title: The flag over Strasbourg
pull: A promise made in the Sahara

facts.text: In early 1941 Free French troops under Colonel Philippe Leclerc crossed the Sahara from French Equatorial Africa and besieged the Italian fort at Kufra in Libya. The Italian and Libyan garrison surrendered on 1 March 1941.
At Kufra Leclerc made his men swear an oath, dated 2 March 1941: "Swear not to lay down your arms until our colours, our beautiful colours, fly over the cathedral of Strasbourg."
By November 1944 Leclerc commanded the French 2nd Armored Division, fighting under the U.S. XV Corps of Gen. Wade Haislip, which broke through the Saverne Gap in the Vosges on 22 November.
At dawn on 23 November the division drove on Strasbourg in several columns, guided by Alsatian resistance fighters. The aim was the Rhine and the bridge to Kehl.
By mid morning three of the columns were stopped by the city's ring of forts, linked by ditches and antitank defences.
The column of Lt. Col. Rouvillois, coming in by an unexpected route through Schiltigheim, broke through, caught the defenders by surprise and drove its tanks through the city to the cathedral.
Rouvillois radioed the coded message "Tissu est dans iode", "Tissue is in iodine": his group was inside Strasbourg.
Early that afternoon a spahi of the division, Maurice Lebrun, volunteered to climb the cathedral's 142 m spire and fix an improvised French flag to it. The oath of Kufra was kept.
The Germans blew the Rhine bridge to Kehl before the French could take it.
On 24 November Leclerc presided over a parade on the Place Kleber.

In January 1945, with Germany counterattacking in Alsace, Eisenhower weighed pulling back and leaving Strasbourg undefended. De Gaulle called it a national disaster, and with Churchill's support the city was held.

photoNote: Tier: green. General Philippe Leclerc walking with his cane, his officers behind him, as he came ashore in Normandy with the French 2nd Armored Division. U.S. Army Signal Corps photo by Kaufman, 111-SC-192467 (naId 176888140), dated 2 August 1944 by NARA, field number ETO-HQ-44-9623, use Unrestricted. Saved 1820 x 3860 portrait (print border trimmed). Not Strasbourg: no public domain photo of Leclerc or the flag in Strasbourg on 23 November turned up in NARA or as a green Commons file (the French SCA poster of Leclerc reviewing troops in Strasbourg is Licence Ouverte, not on the green list), so the credit says Normandy, August 1944. A strong face for the card; frame on his face and the cane. Runner up: French Armored Division coming ashore, 111-SC-192468 (naId 176888142), same day.
photoCredit: Gen. Philippe Leclerc lands in Normandy with the French 2nd Armored Division, August 1944. U.S. Army Signal Corps photo, National Archives 111-SC-192467, public domain.

declassified.fact: Strasbourg's German commander, Gen. Franz Vaterrodt, did not give up with the city. He held out in Fort Ney with about 600 men and surrendered only on 25 November.

film.record: Combat Bulletin No. 35 (1944, Army Pictorial Service, Signal Corps), 111-CB-35 (NARA 24321)
film.shot_notes: Whole bulletin, 20 min 17 s, converted from NARA's 640 x 480 WMV to H.264 MP4 (one upload shared with the 27 Nov Saipan card, which uses 00:30 to 02:18). Narration over the whole bulletin, so the clips run silent. The Alsace story opens at 14:15 with an animated map (1st Army Duren, 3rd Army Sarreguemines, 7th Army Strasbourg; avoid). NOON: 16:15 to 19:25, the city and its streets: 16:15 to 16:31 a town seen from a height with the Vosges behind; 16:35 a skyline with a tall chimney and a church spire; 16:39 a soldier aiming from a window; 16:43 black smoke over the town; 16:55 to 17:11 shells bursting along a riverfront; 17:15 to 17:39 houses and a street under fire, a soldier at a fence; 18:19 to 18:27 soldiers in a street; 18:31 to 19:23 tanks rolling down village streets with infantry, half timbered Alsatian houses at 19:03. Open on the tanks in the street (about 18:31) or the shellbursts by the river (16:55). 7 P.M. (second cut): 14:23 to 16:11, the drive across the Alsace plain: 14:27 to 14:31 a tank passing the camera; 14:39 to 14:51 shells bursting on the open plain; 15:11 to 15:19 troops moving across fields; 15:31 a mortar man; 15:35 to 15:59 a howitzer crew firing, a soldier with a mug at 15:51; 16:07 smoke along a hedge. Open on the tank at 14:27 or the gun crew firing at 15:35. The two stretches do not overlap. Caution: the troops wear U.S. helmets and the narration could not be checked here, so the film may show U.S. Seventh Army units as well as Leclerc's men (who also wore U.S. kit); no shot clearly shows the cathedral or a French flag. Ends 19:27 with The End.
film.license: Public domain, U.S. government work (Army Pictorial Service, Signal Corps, NARA Record Group 111).
film.date_note: U.S. Army film of the Seventh Army front in Alsace in November 1944, released in Combat Bulletin 35; the shots are not dated to 23 November and the units are not named on screen, so the caption should say U.S. Army film of the Alsace drive toward Strasbourg, November 1944.

video.note: U.S. Army film of the Seventh Army front in Alsace, November 1944, Combat Bulletin No. 35, 111-CB-35 (NARA 24321). Narration over the bulletin, so the clip runs silent. Cut 19 Nov 2026 from footage/1944-11-23-cb35.mp4, inside research's noon stretch 16:15 to 19:25: 18:31.6 to 18:36.6 an armored vehicle rolls down a village street toward the camera with infantry; 17:01.0 to 17:05.0 shells bursting along a riverfront; 17:17.5 to 17:20.5 armor behind a house under fire; 19:11.0 to 19:14.0 an armored vehicle and a soldier in a street. Vignette edges cropped. Nothing from the 7 p.m. stretch (14:23 to 16:11). Units not named on screen; not dated to 23 November.

Three French columns were stopped at the forts. Another came in by a route nobody expected and drove its tanks to the cathedral.

U.S. Army film of the drive into Alsace toward Strasbourg, November 1944.

What wins more battles, speed or surprise?
